title: The EB-2 Green Card Queue for Indians Just Slammed Shut. It Won't Reopen Until October.
excerpt: The State Department marked EB-2 India 'unavailable' after the final action date retrogressed by more than ten months. Hundreds of thousands of H-1B professionals are stuck in place until the new fiscal year.
body:
The June 2026 Visa Bulletin, released by the U.S. Department of State, delivered the worst possible news for Indian professionals waiting for employment-based green cards: the EB-2 India category has been designated "unavailable." It will not reopen until October 1, when the new fiscal year begins.

The designation means that no Indian-born applicant in the EB-2 category — which covers professionals with advanced degrees or exceptional ability — can have their green card application adjudicated for the remainder of FY2026. The final action date, which had been hovering around mid-2013, retrogressed by more than ten months before the category shut entirely.

EB-1 India, the priority worker category, also slipped backward by roughly three and a half months, moving to December 15, 2022. EB-3, the category for skilled workers and professionals, advanced by a single month to December 15, 2013.

## What "Unavailable" Actually Means

For the roughly 300,000 Indian professionals with pending EB-2 petitions, the practical impact is severe. No final green card approvals can be issued in this category until the new fiscal year opens fresh allocations. USCIS had been using the more generous "Dates for Filing" chart through June, which allowed some applicants to continue filing paperwork. But the State Department warned in its bulletin notes that further retrogression or an unavailable designation could follow — and within weeks, it did.

The root cause is structural. The United States caps employment-based green cards at approximately 140,000 per year, and no single country can receive more than seven percent of that total — roughly 9,800 visas. India, which generates far more qualified applicants than any other country in the EB-2 pipeline, consistently exhausts its allocation well before the fiscal year ends. When demand outstrips supply by this margin, the State Department freezes the queue.

"The heavy filing from India-chargeable applicants forced the cutoff back to hold number use inside the FY2026 limit," immigration advisory firm WR Immigration noted in its analysis. Fragomen, one of the largest immigration law firms globally, warned that the current trajectory could lead to even tighter restrictions in subsequent bulletins.

## A Decade in Limbo

Behind the data are engineers, researchers, physicians, and corporate managers — many of whom have lived in the United States for over a decade on temporary H-1B visas. They pay income taxes at the same rates as citizens. They own homes in cities from San Jose to Seattle to Chicago. They start companies, mentor colleagues, and raise children who were born American. Yet they cannot change employers freely, cannot travel without anxiety over visa stamps, and cannot vote in the country they have helped build.

Consider the timeline. An Indian software engineer who filed her EB-2 labor certification in 2013 — thirteen years ago — is still waiting. A cardiologist who entered the queue in 2014 has watched his American-born children start middle school while his own status remains provisional. The "unavailable" designation does not merely pause their progress. It erases the illusion that progress was being made at all.

The per-country cap has been a persistent target of legislative reform. The EAGLE Act and the Fairness for High-Skilled Immigrants Act both aimed to eliminate or raise it, redistributing unused allocations from low-demand countries to high-demand ones like India and China. Neither bill has survived the full congressional gauntlet. In the current political environment — where a dozen Republican lawmakers have introduced bills to restrict or suspend the H-1B programme itself — prospects for reform appear more distant than ever.

For many Indian professionals abroad, this situation has significant implications. The inability to secure permanent residency affects not only their personal lives but also their ability to contribute to the economy through remittances and investments. Family ties are strained as they navigate uncertain immigration statuses, and the prospect of dual citizenship remains a distant dream for many.

## The Options Left

Immigration attorneys are counselling affected applicants to weigh several imperfect alternatives. An EB-3 downgrade — voluntarily stepping into a lower preference category — offers a marginally more current date of December 15, 2013, but the queue there is almost equally clogged. Some families are pivoting to the EB-5 investor visa programme, where set-aside categories for rural and high-unemployment areas remain current for India-born applicants. The minimum investment is $800,000, placing it beyond reach for most salaried professionals.

A growing cohort is looking outside the United States entirely. Canada's Express Entry system processes skilled immigrants in months, not decades. Australia's points-based visa has attracted tens of thousands of Indian tech workers. The UAE's Golden Visa programme grants ten-year residency to qualified professionals. Each time the American system tightens, these alternatives gain ground.

The October 2026 visa bulletin — reflecting the start of FY2027 and a fresh annual allocation — is the next meaningful checkpoint. When new numbers become available, immigration experts predict EB-2 India dates will jump forward. But the structural backlog, estimated at over a million pending applications across all employment-based categories for India, is not shrinking. It is growing.

The queue is officially closed. Four months of waiting, at minimum, have just been added to a wait that already spans generations.

---

*Sources: U.S. Department of State June 2026 Visa Bulletin, WR Immigration, Fragomen, Shusterman Immigration Law*
